title: Foundations
tagline: Score an AI feature idea against value, viability, feasibility, and usability — reframed for AI.

concept.intro: You already know value, viability, feasibility, and usability. Nothing about those four lenses changes when the feature involves AI — but each one now has an AI-specific question hiding inside it that classic PM training never had to ask.

sections.heading: Value — is AI actually the right mechanism?
sections.body: The bar is the same: does this solve a real problem for a real user? What's new is a second check — is AI the right way to solve it, or is it the fashionable way? A rules engine or a simple form is sometimes the better answer. 'We could use AI here' is not the same claim as 'AI is the best way to solve this.'

sections.heading: Viability — cost of inference, not just cost of build
sections.body: Classic viability asks whether the business case closes. AI viability adds a cost that scales with usage: every model call has a marginal cost (tokens in, tokens out). A feature that's cheap to build can still be expensive to run at scale. You also now have a build-vs-buy-vs-prompt decision — do you fine-tune a model, call a vendor API, or just write a very good prompt against an existing model?

sections.heading: Feasibility — model limits, data readiness, and evals before code
sections.body: Feasibility used to mostly mean engineering capacity. Now it also means: do we have the data this needs, and is it clean enough to use? Can the model reliably do this task at all? And critically — how will we know if it's working? Eval-driven development means defining your success criteria and test cases *before* you build, not writing a rubric after something ships and looks wrong.

sections.heading: Usability — designing for the moment the model is wrong
sections.body: Every AI feature will sometimes be wrong. Usability now includes: does the user know when to trust the output? Is there a graceful way to correct it? Is there a clear point where a human needs to step back in? An AI feature with no visible 'this might be wrong, here's how to fix it' path is a usability gap, not just an accuracy gap.

sections.heading: Two more lenses you'll build in later weeks
sections.body: Autonomy level (how much can the AI decide on its own — you'll use this in Week 3) and context engineering (the constraint file that keeps an AI agent inside scope — also Week 3) round out the picture. This week is just the four classics, sharpened.

scenario.context: Northwind Gear Co. is a fictional outdoor-gear e-commerce retailer. Customer support is spending significant time drafting return-approval responses by hand, checking each request against a return policy document.
scenario.brief: Feature idea under review: an 'AI Returns Assistant' that reads a customer's return request and Northwind's return policy, then drafts a response — either approving the return with instructions, or explaining why it doesn't qualify. A human support agent reviews and sends every drafted response before it goes out.

exercise.instructions: Score the AI Returns Assistant idea against each of the four lenses below. One or two sentences of rationale per lens is enough — the goal is the habit of asking the AI-specific question, not a long essay.

prompts.label: Value
prompts.help: Is AI the right mechanism here, or would a simpler tool (e.g. a decision-tree form) solve this just as well?
prompts.placeholder: e.g. Return policy has enough exceptions and free-text nuance that a rules engine would be brittle. AI drafting, human approving, is a reasonable fit because...

prompts.label: Viability
prompts.help: What does this cost to run at Northwind's support volume, and is prompting an existing model enough, or does this need something heavier?
prompts.placeholder: e.g. At ~2,000 return requests/week, per-call cost is low relative to agent time saved. A well-prompted existing model should be sufficient — no fine-tuning needed to start.

prompts.label: Feasibility
prompts.help: Is the policy data clean enough to ground the model? What would you test before trusting this in production?
prompts.placeholder: e.g. Policy doc needs to be the single source of truth and kept current. Before launch, run 50 historical return requests through it and compare drafts to what agents actually decided.

prompts.label: Usability
prompts.help: How does a support agent know when to trust a draft versus double-check it? What's the correction path?
prompts.placeholder: e.g. Every draft shows the policy section it cited, so the agent can verify at a glance. Anything involving a VIP account or an amount over $500 is flagged for closer review before sending.
